title: Headless & Automation
description: Run Claude without the chat UI: claude -p, output formats, pipes, scripts and CI.

lessons.title: claude -p Basics
lessons.description: One prompt in, one answer out

theory.title: Print mode
theory.body:
`claude -p "query"` (long form `--print`) runs Claude **non-interactively**: it does the task, prints the result, and exits. No chat window, no follow-up questions. Kip calls this "going headless" (the shell stays on).

Put the prompt in quotes right after `-p` so the shell passes it as one piece of text.

Add `-c` (long form `--continue`) to send a follow-up to your **most recent conversation** instead of starting a new one.

When it finishes, `claude -p` gives an **exit code**: `0` means success, anything else means it failed. Scripts check this number to decide what to do next.
theory.code:
# one question, one answer
claude -p "What does the auth module do?"

# follow up in the most recent conversation
claude -c -p "Now check for type errors"

theory.title: Pipes and redirects
theory.body:
Command-line programs read input (**stdin**) and write output (**stdout**). Three symbols wire them together:

`|` (pipe): send the output of the command on the left into the command on the right. `cat logs.txt` prints a file, so `cat logs.txt | claude -p "..."` hands that file to Claude.

`< file`: feed a file in as input. Same effect as `cat file |`.

`> file`: save the output to a file instead of printing it.
theory.code:
# pipe a file in
cat build-error.txt | claude -p "explain the root cause"

# same thing with <
claude -p "explain the root cause" < build-error.txt

# save the answer to output.txt
cat build-error.txt | claude -p "explain the root cause" > output.txt

theory.title: Output formats and jq
theory.body:
`--output-format` picks the shape of the output:

`text` (default): plain text for humans.

`json`: one JSON object. The answer is in the `result` field; there's also `session_id` and `total_cost_usd` (estimated spend).

`stream-json`: one JSON event per line, live as the run happens (pair it with `--verbose`).

`--json-schema` goes further: Claude's output is validated against a JSON schema you provide.

`jq` is a small tool that pulls fields out of JSON: `jq -r '.result'` prints just the `result` field (`.result`), as raw text without quotes (`-r`).
theory.code:
# the json output looks roughly like
{ "result": "This project is...", "session_id": "...", "total_cost_usd": 0.01 }

# keep only the answer text
claude -p "Summarize this project" --output-format json | jq -r '.result'

exercises.prompt: Which output format streams newline-delimited JSON events in real time?
exercises.explanation: `stream-json` sends each event as it happens, so a script can show progress instead of waiting for the final answer.

exercises.prompt: In `--output-format json`, which field reports the estimated spend for the run?
exercises.explanation: JSON output carries metadata like `total_cost_usd` next to the answer, so scripts can track spend without parsing text.

exercises.prompt: How can a shell script tell whether a `claude -p` run failed?
options: Parse the word 'error' from the output
Check the exit code: 0 on success, non-zero on failure
exercises.explanation: Exit codes are how every command-line program reports success, so checking for 0 is more reliable than reading the text.

exercises.prompt: Match each flag value to what you get.
exercises.explanation: Pick by who reads the output: text for humans, json for scripts, stream-json for live progress, --json-schema for a guaranteed shape.

exercises.prompt: A script pipes a failed build log into Claude and saves the answer for the team.
options: cat build.log | claude -p "concisely explain the root cause of this build error and name the file to fix"
exercises.explanation: Nobody can answer follow-up questions in a script, so the prompt itself must say exactly what output you want.

exercises.prompt: Get JSON output and extract just the answer text with jq.
exercises.hint: --output-format json, then jq -r '.<field>' where the answer field is named result.
exercises.explanation: jq can only read JSON, so you ask for json output and then pick the `result` field, which is where the answer lives.

exercises.prompt: Run Claude non-interactively with the prompt "summarize this project" (include the quotes).
exercises.explanation: `-p` makes Claude answer once and exit, which is what lets it run inside scripts with nobody watching.

exercises.prompt: Use a pipe to send the contents of logs.txt into Claude with the prompt "explain these errors".
exercises.explanation: Print mode reads stdin, so whatever you pipe in becomes part of what Claude sees alongside your prompt.

exercises.prompt: Continue your most recent conversation headlessly with the prompt "Now focus on the database queries".
accepted: claude -c -p "Now focus on the database queries"
claude --continue -p "Now focus on the database queries"
claude -c --print "Now focus on the database queries"
claude --continue --print "Now focus on the database queries"
claude -p "Now focus on the database queries" --continue
claude -p "Now focus on the database queries" -c
exercises.explanation: `-c` keeps the earlier conversation as context, so a script can build on a previous answer instead of starting over.

theory.title: Guardrails for unattended runs
theory.body:
Nobody is around to click "allow" in a script, so decide permissions up front:

`--allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"`: these tools run without asking. You can narrow one with a rule like `Bash(git diff *)`. `--disallowedTools` denies or removes tools.

`--max-turns 3`: stop after 3 agentic turns (print mode only), so a run can't go on forever.

`--append-system-prompt "..."`: **adds** your instructions and keeps Claude Code's default system prompt. `--system-prompt` **replaces** the default entirely.

`--bare`: skip auto-discovered hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md for reproducible CI runs.

Use `--dangerously-skip-permissions` only inside an isolated container.
theory.code:
claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"

claude -p "fix the lint errors" --max-turns 3

theory.title: Reading a script
theory.body:
A few shell pieces show up in scripts:

`\` at the end of a line: the command continues on the next line. It's just for readability.

`"$1"`: the first argument given to the script. Run `./review.sh 42` and `$1` is `42`.

`gh pr diff 42`: print the diff of pull request 42 (GitHub CLI).

`2>&1`: also send error messages into the pipe. Test runners often print failures as errors, which a plain `|` would skip.
theory.code:
# review.sh: run as ./review.sh 42
gh pr diff "$1" | claude -p \
  --append-system-prompt "You are a test engineer. List missing tests." \
  --output-format json

# include error output in the pipe
npm test 2>&1 | claude -p "summarize the failures"

theory.title: Claude in GitHub Actions
theory.body:
The `anthropics/claude-code-action` runs Claude in GitHub's automation (workflows). Mention `@claude` in an issue or PR comment and it gets to work.

Fastest setup: run `/install-github-app` inside a session. It installs the Claude GitHub App, saves your key as a repo secret (like `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`), and prepares the workflow PR.

Workflows are written in **YAML**: `key: value` pairs, where indentation shows what belongs inside what, and `- ` starts a list item. `uses:` names the action as `owner/name@version`. `with:` gives it inputs. `${{ secrets.NAME }}` inserts a secret without writing it in the file. CLI flags go in `claude_args`.
theory.code:
- uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1   # which action, version 1
  with:                                     # its inputs:
    anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
    claude_args: "--max-turns 5"            # normal CLI flags

options: Append keeps Claude Code's default prompt and adds yours; --system-prompt replaces it entirely
Append only works in interactive mode
--system-prompt adds text to the end of every user message
exercises.explanation: Appending keeps the default tool and safety guidance Claude relies on, while replacing drops all of it.

options: On your laptop, to save time
Inside an isolated container or sandbox with nothing valuable to damage
exercises.explanation: It skips every permission check, so it's only safe where a mistake can't reach real files, systems or secrets.

exercises.prompt: Match each flag to its job in a script.
exercises.explanation: With no human watching, these flags decide in advance what Claude may do, for how long, and under which instructions.

exercises.prompt: Complete review.sh: security-review a PR diff and return JSON.
exercises.code:
gh pr diff "$1" | claude ___ \
  --___ "You are a security engineer. Review for vulnerabilities." \
  --output-format ___
exercises.hint: Same shape as review.sh in the theory: claude -p, --append-system-prompt "role", --output-format json.
exercises.explanation: `-p` is what lets Claude read the piped diff, the appended prompt sets the reviewer role, and json makes the result easy for scripts to use.

exercises.code:
- uses: anthropics/___@v1
  with:
    anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
    claude_args: "--___ 5"
exercises.hint: uses: owner/name@version. claude_args holds normal CLI flags, like the one that caps turns.
exercises.explanation: `uses` must name the real action, anthropics/claude-code-action, and claude_args takes the same flags as the CLI, so --max-turns caps the run.

exercises.prompt: Order the quick setup for @claude in GitHub.
steps: Install the gh CLI and run gh auth login
Open claude in the repo and run /install-github-app
Let it install the Claude GitHub App and save the secret
Create and merge the workflow pull request it prepares
Mention @claude in an issue or PR comment
exercises.explanation: The setup talks to GitHub through gh, and the workflow only runs once its PR is merged, so @claude comes last.

exercises.prompt: Headlessly run the prompt "Run the test suite and fix any failures", pre-approving the tools "Bash,Read,Edit" (keep both quoted).
accepted: claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"
claude --print "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit"
claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowed-tools "Bash,Read,Edit"
claude --print "Run the test suite and fix any failures" --allowed-tools "Bash,Read,Edit"
exercises.explanation: A script can't answer permission prompts, so `--allowedTools` approves the needed tools before the run starts.

exercises.prompt: Headlessly run the prompt "fix the lint errors", limited to 3 agentic turns.
exercises.explanation: Capping turns stops an unattended run that's going in circles before it burns time and money.

exercises.prompt: Inside a session, type the slash command that starts the quick setup for Claude in GitHub Actions.
exercises.explanation: `/install-github-app` does the app install, secret and workflow PR for you, so you don't have to write the YAML by hand.

exercises.scenario: A nightly CI job pipes `npm test` output into `claude -p`. Write the prompt so the report is useful with nobody around to ask follow-ups.
exercises.sample: npm test 2>&1 | claude -p "Context: these are tonight's CI test results; the test script is defined in @package.json. Goal: for each failing test, give the test name, the likely root cause in one sentence, and the file to look at. Constraints: don't edit any files; output Markdown bullets only, no intro text. Done: one bullet per failing test, or if every test passed, print exactly: ALL GREEN"
exercises.explanation: Nobody can ask follow-ups in CI, so a headless prompt must define the exact output, including what to print when there's nothing to report.

mission.title: Go Headless
mission.intro: Kip unplugs the chat window. Make Claude work as a plain command-line tool in your own scripts.
checklist: Run claude -p "summarize this project" in a repo
Pipe input: git log --oneline -20 | claude -p "summarize these recent commits"
Run a prompt with --output-format json and pipe it to jq -r '.result'
Optional: run /install-github-app in a repo you admin
mission.explanation: Print mode, pipes, JSON output and guardrail flags are the building blocks of every Claude automation.

cheatsheet.description: Run one prompt non-interactively, print, exit (also --print).
Pipe content into Claude via stdin.
Continue the most recent conversation headlessly.
Plain text, one JSON object, or streamed JSON events.
Deny or remove tools for the run.
Limit agentic turns in print mode.
Add instructions while keeping the default system prompt.
Skip auto-discovered config for faster, reproducible scripted runs.
Set up Claude in GitHub Actions for this repo.
Mention in an issue or PR comment to trigger the action.
